nameStory: The name "nasturtium" comes from the Latin words "nasus" (nose) and "tortum" (twisted), literally meaning "nose-twister" — a perfect description of what happens when you take a whiff of these peppery plants! The spicy scent and taste reminded early botanists of watercress, so they borrowed the name, even though garden nasturtiums aren't closely related to true nasturtiums like watercress at all.
description: Garden nasturtium is a cheerful annual flower that brings bright splashes of yellow, orange, and red to New England gardens from summer through fall. This climbing or trailing plant features distinctive round, shield-like leaves that look almost like tiny lily pads, and showy trumpet-shaped flowers with a characteristic spur at the back. The entire plant has a peppery, watercress-like smell and taste, and it typically sprawls along the ground or climbs up supports, reaching 1-3 feet in height. Originally from South America, it's now a beloved garden escape that occasionally pops up in wild spaces.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly round, disc-shaped leaves with smooth edges that feel slightly waxy and have a distinctive peppery smell when crushed — like a cross between watercress and black pepper

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright trumpet-shaped blooms in vivid yellows, oranges, and reds with five irregular petals and a prominent curved spur extending backward from the flower

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Trailing or climbing stems that feel somewhat succulent and hollow, often sprawling along the ground or twining up fences and trellises

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, wrinkled, three-part seeds about the size of a small pea that feel quite hard and have distinctive ridged surfaces

idTips.label: Taste
idTips.description: Both leaves and flowers have a sharp, peppery bite that tingles the tongue — they're completely edible and often used in salads

habitat: Garden nasturtiums are most commonly found as garden escapes near homes, parks, and cultivated areas throughout New England. They prefer well-drained, somewhat poor soils and full to partial sun, often appearing along fence lines, in vacant lots, or naturalized areas where seeds have scattered from nearby gardens. You'll rarely find them in deep woods or wetlands, as they need good light and don't compete well with established native vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring after the last frost, producing the first round leaves. Young plants are just getting established and may not yet have their characteristic peppery smell.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant bright flowers and full foliage development. This is when the peppery scent is strongest and identification is easiest.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until the first hard frost, with seeds developing and ripening. Plants may look somewhat sprawling and tired but flowers persist.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost, leaving only seeds behind. No above-ground parts survive New England winters.

funFact: Garden nasturtium flowers are edible and have been used as a natural antibiotic for centuries — the same compounds that give them their peppery kick actually have antimicrobial properties, making them both a tasty salad garnish and a traditional folk medicine!
confusionNotes: The round leaves might remind you of wild ginger or violet leaves, but nasturtium's leaves smell distinctly peppery when crushed (the others don't), and nasturtiums have bright trumpet flowers rather than small woodland blooms. The peppery smell test is your best friend here!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, garden nasturtiums aren't true nasturtiums at all — they're not related to watercress and other plants in the real nasturtium family. This naming mix-up happened because early botanists thought they smelled similar, but modern science shows they're completely different plant families that just happen to share that peppery chemical compound.
compareHints: Garden nasturtium is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making identification relatively straightforward. Within the broader nasturtium family (Tropaeolaceae), it's distinguished from its tropical relatives by being an annual rather than perennial, and by its specific flower spur shape and climbing habit rather than the more compact growth of some related species.
